babble.e: From Middle English babelen, from Old English *bæblian, also wæflian (“to talk foolishly”), from Proto-West Germanic *bablōn, *wablōn, variants of *babalōn, from Proto-Germanic *babalōną (“to chatter”).
babble.g: To utter words indistinctly or unintelligibly; to utter inarticulate sounds

babbler.e: From Middle English babeler, babler, equivalent to babble + -er.

babbling.e: From Middle English bablyng, babelynge, babelinde, equivalent to babble + -ing.

babe.e: From Middle English babe, a variant of earlier baban, perhaps from Old English *baba (“boy, child”), from Proto-West Germanic *babō, from Proto-Germanic *babô, reduplicated variant of *ba-, *bō- (“father, brother, close male relation”).
babe.g: A baby or infant; a very young human or animal.

babes.g: Alternative form of babe (“as a term of endearment to a loved one”).

baby.e: From Middle English baby, babie (“baby”), a diminutive form of babe (“babe, baby”), equivalent to babe + -y/-ie (“endearing and diminutive suffix”). Perhaps ultimately imitative of baby talk (compare babble).
baby.g: A very young human, particularly from birth to a couple of years old or until walking is fully mastered.

back.e: From Middle English bak, from Old English bæc, from Proto-West Germanic *bak, from Proto-Germanic *baką, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg- (“to bend”). The adverb represents an aphetic form of aback.

back.g: A large shallow vat; a cistern, tub, or trough, used by brewers, distillers, dyers, picklers, gluemakers, and others, for mixing or cooling

backbiting.e: From Middle English bakbytynge, equivalent to backbite + -ing.
backbiting.g: Slanderous or speaking badly, especially of a person without that person's knowledge.

backbone.e: From Middle English bakbon, bakebon, bac-bon; equivalent to back + bone.
backbone.g: The series of vertebrae, separated by disks, that encloses and protects the spinal cord, and runs down the middle of the back in vertebrate

backed.g: Put on one's back; killed; rendered dead.

backside.g: The back side of anything, the part opposite its front, particularly

backslide.g: To regress; to slip backwards or revert to a previous, worse state.

backslider.g: A recidivist; one who backslides, especially in a religious sense; an apostate.

backward.e: From Middle English bakwarde, abakward, equivalent to back (adverb) + -ward.

bad.e: From Middle English bad, from Old English bæd, first- and third-person singular indicative past tense of biddan (“to ask”).

badger.e: From Middle English bageard (“marked by a badge”), from bage (“badge”), referring to the animal's badge-like white blaze, equivalent to badge + -ard.
badger.g: Any member of species of the genera Meles, Arctonyx, Mellivora or Taxidea, of mammals.

badger.e: Unknown Possibly from bagger. "Baggier" is cited by the OED in 1467-8.
badger.g: An itinerant licensed dealer in commodities used for food; a hawker or huckster; especially one who bought grain in one place and sold it in

badly.e: From Middle English badly, baddely, baddeliche, equivalent to bad + -ly.

badness.e: From Middle English baddenes, badnes, badnesse; equivalent to bad + -ness.
badness.g: The quality or degree of being bad.

baffle.e: The origin of the verb is uncertain; it is possibly: from French bafouer, baffoüer (“to abuse, revile; to confuse, baffle; to deceive; to flout; to scorn”), imitative of someone making a disdainful sound by expelling air quickly through pouted lips (compare Occitan baf (interjection expressing disdain)).
baffle.g: To confuse or perplex (someone) completely; to bewilder, to confound, to puzzle.

baffle.e: The origin of the verb is uncertain; it is possibly from Scots bauchle (“to annoy; to cause harm or trouble to; to disgrace; to jilt; to treat with contempt”), from bauchle (“useless or worn-out person or thing; clumsy work, bungle; clumsy or untidy person; contemptible person; laughing stock”).
baffle.g: To publicly disgrace (someone); specifically, a recreant knight.

bag.e: From Middle English bagge, from Old Norse baggi (“bag, pack, satchel, bundle”) (whence also Old French bague (“bundle, package, sack”)); related to Old Norse bǫggr (“harm, shame; load, burden”), of uncertain origin.
bag.g: A soft container made out of cloth, paper, thin plastic, etc. and open at the top, used to hold food, commodities, and other goods.

baggage.e: From Middle English bagage, from Old French bagage, baguage, from bague (“bundle, sack”), of Germanic/North Germanic origin, probably from the same ultimate source as Old Norse baggi (“pack, bundle”). By surface analysis, bag + -age. The old meaning of "nasty woman" likely derives from the sense of "something awkward to be carried" (compare faggot).
baggage.g: Portable cases, large bags, and similar equipment for manually carrying, pushing, or pulling personal items while traveling

bags.e: Grammatical extension of third-person singular form of bag (“make first claim on something”).

bah.e: Early 19th century, probably borrowed from French bah.
bah.g: Expressing contempt, disgust, or bad temper.

bait.e: From Middle English bayte, bait, beite, from Old Norse beita (“food, bait”), from Proto-Germanic *baitō (“that which is bitten, bait”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to cleave, split, separate”).
bait.g: Any substance, especially food, used in catching fish, or other animals, by alluring them to a hook, snare, trap, or net.

bait.e: From Middle English bayten, baiten, beiten, from Old Norse beita (“to bait, cause to bite, feed, hunt”), from Proto-Germanic *baitijaną (“to cause to bite, bridle”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to cleave, split, separate”).
bait.g: To set dogs on (an animal etc.) to bite or worry; to attack with dogs, especially for sport.

bake.e: From Middle English baken, from Old English bacan (“to bake”), from Proto-West Germanic *bakan, from Proto-Germanic *bakaną (“to bake”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₃g- (“to roast, bake”).
bake.g: To cook using an oven, especially baked goods.

bakemeat.e: From Middle English bake mete, baken mete; equivalent to bake + meat.
bakemeat.g: Any baked product (such as a pie)

baker.e: From Middle English bakere, from Old English bæcere (“baker”), from Proto-Germanic *bakārijaz (“baker”), equivalent to bake + -er.
baker.g: A person who bakes and sells bread, cakes and similar items.

baking.e: From Middle English bakynge; equivalent to bake + -ing.

balance.e: From Middle English balaunce, from Old French balance, from Late Latin *bilancia, from (accusative form of) Latin bilanx (“two-scaled”), from bi- + lanx (“plate, scale”).
balance.g: A state in which opposing forces harmonise; equilibrium.

bald.e: From Middle English balled, ballid, bald (“bald”), of uncertain origin. Probably formed from Middle English bal, balle (“ball, round object, knoll, head”). An alternate etymology relates it to Old English bǣl (“fire, flame; funeral pyre”), from Proto-Germanic *bēlą.
bald.g: Having little or no hair, fur, or feathers.

baldhead.g: A person whose head is bald.

baldness.e: From Middle English ballednesse, equivalent to bald + -ness.
baldness.g: The condition or state of being (or becoming) bald.

ball.e: From Middle English bal, ball, balle, from an unattested Old English *beall, *bealla (“round object, ball”), from Proto-Germanic *balluz, *ballô (“ball”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰol-n- (“ball, bubble”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to blow, inflate, swell”). Ballen (“bale”)). Related forms in Romance are borrowings from Germanic.
ball.g: A solid or hollow sphere, or roughly spherical mass.

ball.e: From Middle French bal, from Middle French baler (“to dance”), from Old French baller, from Late Latin ballō (“to dance”).

balm.e: From Middle English bawme, borrowed from Anglo-Norman and Middle French baume, from Old French basme, from Latin balsamum, itself from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon). Spelling modified 16th c. to conform to Latin etymology.
balm.g: Any of various aromatic resins exuded from certain plants, especially trees of the genus Commiphora of Africa, Arabia and India and Myroxylo

balsam.e: Borrowed from Latin balsamum, from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon, “balsam”), of Semitic origin (Hebrew בושם (“spice, perfume”)); compare Old English balsam, balsamum (“balsam, balm”), Doublet of balm and desman. Not related to balsa.
balsam.g: A sweet-smelling oil or resin derived from various plants.

ban.e: From Middle English bannen (“to summon; to banish; to curse”), partly from Old English bannan (“to summon, command, proclaim, call out”), from Proto-West Germanic *bannan; and partly from Old Norse banna (“to prohibit; to curse”), both from Proto-Germanic *bannaną (“to proclaim, to order; to summon; to ban; to curse, forbid”).
ban.g: To prohibit; to interdict; to proscribe; to forbid or block from participation.

ban.e: Borrowed from Romanian ban of uncertain origin, perhaps from Serbo-Croatian bân.
ban.g: A subdivision of currency, equal to one hundredth of a Romanian leu.

band.e: From Middle English band (also bond), from Old English beand, bænd, bend (“bond, chain, fetter, band, ribbon, ornament, chaplet, crown”), from Proto-Germanic *bandą, *bandiz (“band, fetter”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to tie, bind”). Middle English band reinforced by Old French bande.
band.g: A strip of material used for strengthening or coupling.

band.e: From Middle English band, from Old French bande, from Old Occitan banda (“regiment of troops”), perhaps from Frankish *bend, from Proto-Germanic *bandiz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to tie; bond, band”).
band.g: A group of musicians who perform together as an ensemble; sometimes, such a group working for a professional recording artist.

bandit.e: Borrowed from Italian bandito (“outlawed”), a derivative of Italian bandire (“to ban”), from Late Latin bandīre, an alteration (due to Gothic 𐌱𐌰𐌽𐌳𐍅𐌾𐌰𐌽 (bandwjan, “to signal”)) of Late Latin bannīre (“to ban”), from Frankish *bannan (“to ban”).
bandit.g: One who robs others in a lawless area, especially as part of a group.

banish.e: From Middle English banishen, from Old French baniss-, extended stem of banir (“to proclaim, ban, banish”), of Germanic origin and Old English bannan, from Proto-Germanic *bannaną (“curse, forbid”).
banish.g: To send (someone) away and forbid them from returning.

bank.e: From Middle English banke, from Middle French banque, from Italian banca (“counter, moneychanger's bench or table”), from Lombardic bank (“bench, counter”), from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench, counter”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg- (“to turn, curve, bend, bow”).
bank.g: An institution where one can place and borrow money and take care of financial affairs.

bank.e: From Middle English bank, banke, from Old English *banca (“bench”) (attested in Old English hōbanca (“couch”) and Old English banc (“bank, hillock, embankment”), from Proto-West Germanic *bankō, from Proto-Germanic *bankô.
bank.g: An edge of river, lake, or other watercourse.

banker.g: One who conducts the business of banking; one who, individually, or as a member of a company, keeps an establishment for the deposit or loan

banker.e: From bank (“an elevation, or rising ground”) + -er (relational noun suffix) or + -er (occupational suffix).
banker.g: A vessel employed in the cod fishery on the banks of Newfoundland.

banner.e: From Middle English baner, from Old French baniere (Modern bannière), of Germanic origin.
banner.g: A flag or standard used by a military commander, monarch or nation.

banquet.e: From Middle English banket, from Middle French banquet, from Italian banchetto (“light repast between meals, snack eaten on a small bench”, literally “a small bench”), from banco (“bench”), from Lombardic *bank, *panch (“bench”), from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench”). The unetymological /w/ resulted from spelling-pronunciation.
banquet.g: A large celebratory meal; a feast.

baptism.e: From Middle English bapteme, baptesme, from Old French batesme or bapteme, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptisma, from Ancient Greek βάπτισμα (báptisma, “dipping, baptism”), from βαπτίζω (baptízō, “I dip in liquid”).
baptism.g: A Christian sacrament, by which one is received into a church and sometimes given a name, generally involving the candidate to be anointed w

baptize.e: From Middle English baptisen, baptizen, from Old French baptiser, batisier, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptizāre, from Ancient Greek βαπτίζω (baptízō, “to immerse, plunge, baptize”).
baptize.g: To perform the sacrament of baptism by immersing someone in water or sprinkling or pouring water over them.
baptize.sf: From Ancient Greek βαπτίζω (baptízō, “to immerse, plunge, baptize”)

bar.e: From Middle English barre, from Old French barre (“beam, bar, gate, barrier”), from Vulgar Latin *barra, of uncertain origin.
bar.g: A solid, more or less rigid object of metal or wood with a uniform cross-section smaller than its length.

bar.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek βάρος (báros, “weight”), as a variant of earlier barye and barad.
bar.g: A non-SI unit of pressure equal to 100,000 pascals, i.e. a megadyne per square centimetre.

barb.e: From Middle English barbe, from Middle French barbe, from Old French barbe (“beard, beard-like element”).
barb.g: The point that stands backward in an arrow, fishhook, etc., to prevent it from being easily extracted. Hence: Anything which stands out with
The Barbary horse, a superior breed introduced from Barbary into Spain by the Moors.

barbarian.e: From Middle English barbarian, borrowed from Medieval Latin barbarinus (“Berber, pagan, foreigner”), from Latin barbaria (“foreign country”), from barbarus (“foreigner, savage”), from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros, “foreign, non-Greek, strange”), possibly onomatopoeic (mimicking foreign languages, akin to English blah blah).
barbarian.g: Relating to people, countries, or customs perceived as uncivilized or inferior.
barbarian.sf: From Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros, “foreign, non-Greek, strange”)

barbarous.e: Late Middle English, from Latin barbarus (“foreigner, savage”), from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros, “foreign, strange”).

barber's.g: Synonym of barbershop (“place of business of a barber”).

barefoot.e: From Middle English barefote, barfot, from Old English bærfōt (“barefoot”), from Proto-West Germanic *baʀafōt, from Proto-Germanic *bazafōts (“barefoot”) equivalent to bare + foot.

barely.e: From Middle English baarly, bareliche, barely, barly, from Old English bærlīċe, equivalent to bare + -ly.

bargain.e: From Middle English bargaynen (“to bargain, make a pledge for sale”), from Old French bargaigner (“to bargain”), from Frankish *borganjan (“to borrow, lend”), from Proto-Germanic *burgijaną (“to borrow, lend”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰergʰ- (“to protect, secure”).
bargain.g: An agreement between parties concerning the sale of property; or a contract by which one party binds themself to transfer the right to some

bark.e: From Middle English barken, berken, borken, from Old English beorcan (“to bark”), from the Proto-West Germanic *berkan (“to bark”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerg- (“to make a noise, growl, bark”), from *bʰer- (“to drone, hum, buzz”). For the noun, compare Old English beorc, bearce (“barking”).
bark.g: To make a short, loud, explosive noise with the vocal organs (said of animals, especially dogs).

bark.e: From Middle English barke (“boat”), from Middle French barque, from Late Latin barca, a regular syncope of Vulgar Latin *barica, from Classical Latin bāris, from Ancient Greek βᾶρις (bâris, “Egyptian boat”), from Coptic ⲃⲁⲁⲣⲉ (baare, “small boat”), from Demotic Egyptian br, from Egyptian bꜣjrb-bA-A-y:r*Z1-P1 (“transport ship”).
bark.g: A small sailing vessel, e.g. a pinnace or a fishing smack; a rowing boat or barge.

barley.e: From Middle English barly, barli, from Old English bærlīċ (“barley-like”, adjective) (later referring to barley itself and grain crops of similar appearance), from bere (“barley”) (compare Scots bere (“six-rowed barley”)), from Proto-Germanic *baraz (compare Old Norse barr), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰers- (“spike, prickle”). Equivalent to bere + -ly.
barley.g: A cereal of the species Hordeum vulgare or its grains, often used as food or to make beer and other malted drinks.

barn.e: From Middle English barn, bern, bærn, from Old English bearn, bern, contracted forms of Old English berern, bereærn (“barn, granary”), compound of bere (“barley”) and ærn, ræn (“dwelling, barn”), from Proto-West Germanic *raʀn, from Proto-Germanic *razną (compare Old Norse rann), from pre-Germanic *h₁rh̥₁-s-nó-.
barn.g: A building, often found on a farm, used for storage or keeping animals such as cattle.

barn.e: From Middle English barn, bern, from Old English bearn (“child, son, offspring, progeny”) and Old Norse barn (“child”).

barrack.e: Borrowed from French baraque, from Spanish barraca or Catalan barraca, which is of uncertain origin. It is probably either a diminutive of Vulgar Latin *barra (“bar”), of unclear origin, or a diminutive of Vulgar Latin *barrum (“clay, mud”) from Celtiberian or Paleo-Hispanic.
barrack.g: A building for soldiers, especially within a garrison; originally referred to temporary huts, now usually to a permanent structure or set of

barrel.e: From Middle English barel, from Anglo-Norman baril, Old French baril, bareil (“barrel”), of uncertain origin. An attempt to link baril to Old French barre (“bar, bolt”) (compare Medieval Latin barra (“bar, rod”)) via assumed Vulgar Latin *barrīculum meets the phonological requirement, but fails to connect the word semantically.
barrel.g: A round (cylindrical) vessel, such as a cask, of greater length than breadth, and bulging in the middle, made of staves bound with hoops, an

barren.e: From Middle English bareyne, from Anglo-Norman baraigne, baraing (“sterile; barren”), of obscure origin; probably from a Germanic language, perhaps Frankish *baʀ (“bare; barren”), from Proto-Germanic *bazaz (“bare”). If so, a cognate of English bare.
barren.g: Not bearing children, childless; hence also unable to bear children, sterile.

barrenness.e: From Middle English bareynnesse; equivalent to barren + -ness.
barrenness.g: The property of being barren; the property of not supporting life.

barrier.e: From Middle English barrer, barrere, barryȝer, from Anglo-Norman barrere (compare French barrière), from barre (“bar”).

barter.e: Late Middle English, from Old French barater.
barter.g: An exchange of goods or services without the use of money.

base.e: From Middle English base, bas, baas, from Old French base, from Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis).
base.g: Something from which other things extend; a foundation.

base.e: From Middle English base, bas, from Old French bas, from Late Latin bassus (“low”).

based.e: A reference to freebase cocaine, via basehead. Coined by American rapper from California Lil B in 2010 to describe his lifestyle.
based.g: Not caring what others think about one's personality, style, or behavior; focused on maintaining individuality.

basin.e: From Middle English basyn, from Old French bacin, from Vulgar Latin *baccinum (“wide bowl”).
basin.g: A wide bowl for washing, sometimes affixed to a wall.

basis.e: From Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷémtis, derived from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- (whence also come).

bask.e: From Middle English basken, from Old Norse baðask (“to take a bath”, literally “to bathe oneself”), mediopassive form from underlying baða (“to bathe”) + sik (“oneself”), from Proto-Germanic *baþōną and *sek.
bask.g: To bathe in warmth; to be exposed to pleasant heat.

basket.e: From Middle English basket, from Anglo-Norman baschet, basket, bascat, from latin bascauda. One theory is that it derives from Late Latin bascauda (“kettle, table-vessel”), from Proto-Brythonic (in Breton baskodenn), from Proto-Celtic *baskis (“bundle, load”).
basket.g: A lightweight woven container, generally round, open at the top, and tapering toward the bottom.

basketful.e: From Middle English basket ful, baskett full, equivalent to basket + -ful.
basketful.g: The amount that will fit into a basket

bastard.e: From Middle English bastard, bastarde, from Old English bastard (used as an epithet), from Anglo-Norman bastard, Old French bastart (“illegitimate child”), perhaps via Medieval Latin bastardus, of obscure origin. Likely from Frankish *bāst (“marriage, relationship”) + Old French -ard, -art (pejorative suffix denoting a specific quality or condition).
bastard.g: A person who was born out of wedlock, and hence often considered an illegitimate descendant.

bat.e: Variant of Middle English bakke, of North Germanic origin (akin to Danish aftenbakke and Swedish nattbacka, both now dialectal). Swedish also has nattblacka, and Icelandic has leðurblaka, in which the second element is a derivative of blaka (“to flap”), but it is unclear whether this word is also the source of bakke, backa, etc.
bat.g: Any flying mammal of the order Chiroptera, usually small and nocturnal, insectivorous or frugivorous.

bat.e: From Middle English batten, baten (“to beat”), from Old French batre (“to beat”), from Late Latin battere, from Latin battuere, of uncertain origin; perhaps of Germanic or Celtic origin. In modern English reinterpreted as a verbal derivative of Etymology 2.
bat.g: To hit with a bat or (figuratively) as if with a bat.

batch.e: From Middle English bach, bache, bahche, from Old English *bæċċ (“something baked”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-West Germanic *bakku, from Proto-Germanic *bakkuz (“baking, baked goods”), cognate with Middle High German becke (“something baked, pastry, baking, bakery”).
batch.g: The quantity of bread or other baked goods baked at one time.

batch.e: From Middle English bache, bæcche, from Old English bæċ, beċe (“brook, stream”).

bath.e: From Middle English bath, baþ, from Old English bæþ (“bath”), from Proto-West Germanic *baþ, from Proto-Germanic *baþą (“bath”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₁- (“to warm”). Corresponding inherited verbs are beath and bathe.
bath.g: A tub or pool which is used for bathing: bathtub.
A former Hebrew unit of liquid volume (about 23 L or 6 gallons).

bathe.e: From Middle English bathen, from Old English baþian (“to bathe, wash”), from Proto-West Germanic *baþōn, from Proto-Germanic *baþōną (“to bathe”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₁- (“to warm”).
bathe.g: To clean oneself by immersion in water or using water; to take a bath, have a bath.

bathing.e: From Middle English bathynge; equivalent to bathe + -ing.
bathing.g: The act of taking a bath.

batter.e: From Middle English batteren, batren, bateren, a frequentative of Middle English batten, baten (“to beat”), equivalent to bat + -er (frequentative suffix).
batter.g: To hit or strike violently and repeatedly.

batter.e: From Middle English bature, from Old French bateure (“the action of beating”), from batre (“to beat”).
batter.g: A beaten mixture of flour and liquid (usually egg and milk), used for baking (e.g. pancakes, cake, or Yorkshire pudding) or to coat food (e.

battle.e: From Middle English batel, batell, batelle, batayle, bataylle, borrowed from Old French bataille, from Late Latin battālia, variant of battuālia (“fighting and fencing exercises”) from Latin battuō (“to strike, hit, beat, fight”), of uncertain origin.

From Early Modern English batell, probably from Middle English *batel (“flourishing”), from Old English *batol (“improving, tending to be good”), from batian (“to get better, improve”) + -ol ( + -le).
battle.g: Of grass or pasture: nutritious to cattle or sheep; fattening, nourishing.

battlement.e: From Middle English batilment, from Old French bataillement, earlier bastillement (“fortification”), from bastillier (“to fortify, to equip with battlements”), from bastille (“fortress”) (see bastion). By surface analysis, battle + -ment.
battlement.g: In fortification: an indented parapet, formed by a series of rising members called cops or merlons, separated by openings called crenelles o

bay.e: From French baie, from Late Latin baia, probably ultimately from Iberian or Basque badia. Partly displaced native Old English byht, whence bight.
bay.g: A body of water (especially the sea) contained by a concave shoreline.

bay.e: From Middle English baye, baie, from Old English beġ (“berry”), as in beġbēam (“berry-tree”), conflated with Old French baie, from Latin bāca (“berry”).
bay.g: A tree or shrub of species Laurus nobilis (family Lauraceae), having dark green leaves and berries.

bid.e: From Middle English bidden, from Old English biddan (“to ask, demand”), from Proto-West Germanic *biddjan, from Proto-Germanic *bidjaną (“to ask”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰedʰ-. Conflated with Old English bēodan (“to offer, announce”) (see Etymology 2 below).
bid.g: To issue a command; to tell.

bid.e: From Middle English beden, from Old English bēodan (“to offer, announce”), from Proto-Germanic *beudaną (“to offer”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- (“be awake, aware”). Conflated with Old English biddan (“to ask, demand”) (see Etymology 1 above).
bid.g: To make an offer to pay or accept a certain price.
